en.title: The house and its rooms
en.goal: Describe a house and say what there is (and isn't) in it.

lessons.porta-janela-tem-nao-tem: Door, window and saying what there is or isn't

phrases.scenario: Someone asks how many bedrooms your small apartment has, and it has only one. What do you say?
You're describing your house, which has two bathrooms. What do you say?
Someone asks if your apartment has a garden, and it doesn't. What do you answer?

il-y-a-vs-negation.title: "Il y a" or "il n'y a pas de"?
il-y-a-vs-negation.body: Il y a (there is / there are) introduces something that exists: il y a une chambre (there is a bedroom). In the negative, the article becomes de, just like in the "food" and "quantities" units: il n'y a pas de jardin (there isn't a garden) — never "il n'y a pas un jardin".

il-y-a-ya.title: In everyday speech, "il y a" becomes "y'a"
il-y-a-ya.body: In fast speech, the "il" in il y a almost disappears — only y'a is left: "y'a une chambre", "y'a pas de jardin". It's so common that it even shows up in informal written messages. In the exercises here, keep writing the full "il y a" — it's the form the exercises ask for.

andar-terreo-premier-etage.title: "1er étage" is not the ground floor
andar-terreo-premier-etage.body: In France, the ground floor has its own name: le rez-de-chaussée. The counting only starts after it — le premier étage is what Americans call the second floor (one floor above the ground floor). (In the UK, "first floor" already matches.) It's worth paying attention to this when looking for an address or taking the elevator.

review.pt: o que, no Brasil, chamaríamos de "segundo andar"
review.en: what Americans call the second floor ... (In the UK, "first floor" already matches.)
review.why: Source said "in Brazil, we would call"; rewritten as a neutral fact about US usage (no "we"). US second floor / UK first floor is correct.
Fragment 'il n'y a pas de' needs the 'any' to reflect 'de' after negation; 'there is no' is an alternative.
'There's no garden.' also correct; kept parallel with the grammar note.

review.pt: O quarto fica no primeiro andar.
review.en: The bedroom is on the first floor.
review.why: In EN-US 'first floor' = ground floor, which clashes with the cultural note (premier étage = one above ground). 'second floor' would be US-accurate but loses the literal match; flag for the teacher.

review.pt: A janela dá para o jardim.
review.en: The window looks out onto the garden.

review.why: Contraction chosen to mirror the colloquial reduction.
